The Westing Game, Ellen Raskin's intricate mystery novel that won the Newbery Medal in nineteen seventy-nine. Sixteen characters are brought together by a will to solve the puzzle of who murdered the eccentric millionaire Samuel Westing. The prize for solving the murder is his enormous estate. The characters are tenants in a new apartment building, and they are divided into pairs and given cryptic clues along with ten thousand dollars each. Their task is to identify Westing's killer within one year and win his fortune. Each pair is connected by a single word or phrase on their clue envelope, which they must interpret to guide their investigation. The puzzle is linguistic as much as narrative. Samuel Westing has designed the game as a kind of will-reading where the characters become detectives, unraveling secrets and connections among themselves. What makes the novel remarkable is its structure. Raskin crafted it so that multiple interpretations are possible, allowing readers to "win" with more than one answer if they reason carefully. The novel is widely praised for its structural ingenuity, its complex characterization of a diverse cast of characters, and the way it rewards careful, active reading. The Westing Game explores human interconnection and reveals how secrets bind communities together. More than anything, it demonstrates the power of games and storytelling to transform lives.
